subject: history
displayName: KS3 History — The Stuarts, Civil War & the Republic
subtitle: The causes and consequences of the English Civil War, the execution of Charles I, and the Restoration.

data.targetWord: the belief that a monarch's authority came directly from God and could not be challenged by Parliament or the people

examples.en-GB: James I used divine right to argue that Parliament had no business questioning his decisions.

data.targetWord: the period from 1629 to 1640 when Charles I governed England without calling Parliament

examples.en-GB: During the Personal Rule, Charles I raised money through Ship Money without Parliament's consent.

data.targetWord: a tax traditionally collected from coastal areas for naval defence, which Charles I controversially extended to inland counties in peacetime without Parliament's consent

examples.en-GB: John Hampden's refusal to pay Ship Money became a famous act of resistance to Charles I's Personal Rule.

data.targetWord: a 1628 document in which Parliament argued that the king should not collect taxes without consent, imprison people without cause, or use martial law in peacetime

examples.en-GB: Charles I accepted the Petition of Right but then ignored its terms, deepening MPs' distrust.

data.targetWord: a supporter of King Charles I during the English Civil War, also known as a Cavalier

examples.en-GB: Royalists believed the king was the lawful ruler and that rebellion would destroy social order.

data.targetWord: a supporter of Parliament during the English Civil War, also known as a Roundhead, who believed Parliament must defend law, liberty and Protestant religion against royal abuse

examples.en-GB: Parliamentarians argued that Charles I had abused his power by raising taxes without consent.

data.targetWord: Parliament's reorganised and professionally disciplined army, created in 1645, which played a decisive role in winning the Civil War

examples.en-GB: The New Model Army's victory at Naseby in 1645 effectively ended Charles I's military position.

data.targetWord: William Laud, Archbishop of Canterbury under Charles I, whose church reforms introduced more ceremony and ritual, alarming many Puritans who feared a return to Catholic practices

examples.en-GB: Archbishop Laud's attempt to impose a new prayer book in Scotland in 1637 triggered a rebellion.

data.targetWord: a war fought between opposing groups within the same country; the English Civil War was between supporters of King Charles I and supporters of Parliament

examples.en-GB: The English Civil War began in 1642 when Charles I raised his royal standard at Nottingham.

data.targetWord: the removal in December 1648 of MPs from Parliament who opposed the army's plan to put Charles I on trial, leaving only those who would support a trial

examples.en-GB: Pride's Purge demonstrated that the army, not Parliament, was the real power in the country by 1648.

data.targetWord: the name given to the English republic established after the execution of Charles I in 1649, when the monarchy and House of Lords were abolished

examples.en-GB: The Commonwealth faced major problems including continued wars, divisions in Parliament, and lack of a settled constitution.

data.targetWord: the period from 1653 to 1658 when Oliver Cromwell ruled England as Lord Protector, holding power with support from the army

examples.en-GB: During the Protectorate, Cromwell tried to create stable government but remained dependent on military power.

data.targetWord: the title held by Oliver Cromwell from 1653, making him the head of state of England without the title of king

examples.en-GB: As Lord Protector, Cromwell had great power but struggled to find a constitutional settlement that Parliament and the army both accepted.

data.targetWord: the return of the monarchy in 1660 when Charles II, son of the executed king, was invited back to rule England

examples.en-GB: The Restoration of 1660 brought back the monarchy, the House of Lords, and the Church of England.

data.targetWord: the events of 1688–1689 when the Catholic king James II was removed and replaced by the Protestant William III and Mary II as joint monarchs

examples.en-GB: The Glorious Revolution is a contested name because violence did occur in Scotland and Ireland during the events.

data.targetWord: the 1689 law that limited the monarch's power by requiring parliamentary consent for taxation and law-making, and stating that Parliament should meet regularly

examples.en-GB: The Bill of Rights of 1689 marked a clear shift in power towards Parliament and away from the Crown.

data.targetWord: the Parliament called by Charles I in 1640, which went on to challenge royal power and pass laws limiting the king's authority

examples.en-GB: The Long Parliament passed laws preventing the king from dissolving it without its own consent.

data.targetWord: a Protestant Christian who wanted the Church of England to be more strictly reformed and free from Catholic ceremony and ritual

examples.en-GB: Many Puritans feared that Laud's religious changes were moving the Church back towards Catholicism.

data.targetWord: a state governed without a monarch, where political power rests with elected representatives or other leaders

examples.en-GB: After the execution of Charles I in 1649, England briefly became a republic called the Commonwealth.

data.targetWord: a change in the fundamental rules, laws or customs that determine how a country is governed and who holds power

examples.en-GB: The Bill of Rights was an example of constitutional change that limited the power of the monarchy.

data.targetWord: the decisive battle of 1645 in which the New Model Army defeated the Royalist forces, effectively ending Charles I's ability to win the Civil War

examples.en-GB: After the Battle of Naseby, Charles I had little hope of military victory and surrendered in 1646.

data.targetWord: the 1644 battle in which Parliament and its Scottish allies won a major victory in the north of England, weakening Royalist control of the region

examples.en-GB: The Battle of Marston Moor showed that Parliament's forces, including Oliver Cromwell's cavalry, could defeat the king's armies.

data.targetWord: the conflicts of 1639–1640 in which Scotland rebelled against Charles I's attempt to impose religious changes, forcing the king to recall Parliament to raise money

examples.en-GB: The Bishops' Wars were a crucial short-term cause of the Civil War because they forced Charles to recall Parliament.

data.targetWord: the broader series of conflicts in the 1640s involving England, Scotland and Ireland, of which the English Civil War was a central part

examples.en-GB: The Wars of the Three Kingdoms shows that the English Civil War was connected to wider conflicts across Britain and Ireland.

data.targetWord: a historian's explanation or judgement about the past, which may differ from other interpretations depending on what evidence is used and which questions are asked

examples.en-GB: Historians have very different interpretations of Oliver Cromwell, some seeing him as a defender of liberty and others as a military tyrant.

data.sentence: Charles I began his ____ in 1629 when he dissolved Parliament and ruled without it for eleven years.
In 1628, Parliament presented Charles I with the ____, arguing that he should not collect taxes or imprison people without proper authority.
Many Puritans feared that Archbishop ____'s religious reforms were moving the Church of England too close to Catholic practices.
Royalists, also known as ____, supported King Charles I during the English Civil War.
Parliament created the ____ in 1645 to create a more disciplined and effective fighting force.
Charles I raised his royal standard at ____ in 1642, marking the formal start of the Civil War.
Charles I was executed outside the Banqueting House in ____ on 30 January 1649.
In December 1648, ____ removed MPs who opposed the army's plans to try Charles I.
Oliver Cromwell became ____ in 1653, holding great power without the title of king.
The monarchy returned in 1660 when ____ was invited back to rule England.
The ____ of 1688–1689 removed the Catholic king James II and replaced him with the Protestant William III and Mary II.
The Bill of Rights of ____ stated that the monarch could not suspend laws without Parliament's consent.
The belief that a king's authority came from God and could not be challenged was called ____.
The decisive Parliamentarian victory at ____ in 1645 destroyed Charles I's main army.
After the execution of Charles I, England became a ____ called the Commonwealth.
Charles I needed to recall Parliament in 1640 because he required money to deal with the Scottish rebellion caused by his attempt to impose a new ____.
Parliament and its Scottish allies won a major victory in the north of England at the Battle of ____ in 1644.
Cromwell's controversial military campaigns in Ireland, especially at Drogheda and Wexford, remain deeply ____ because of the violence and long-term impact.
James II was replaced by ____ and Mary II as joint monarchs in the Glorious Revolution.
The ____ tradition of Scotland resisted Charles I's religious changes because they feared it threatened their Presbyterian church.

data.title: Put the key events of the English Civil War and its aftermath in chronological order
items: Charles I begins Personal Rule without Parliament (1629)
Scottish rebellion forces Charles to recall Parliament (1640)
Civil War breaks out at Nottingham (1642)
New Model Army wins at Naseby (1645)
Charles I is tried and executed (1649)
Oliver Cromwell becomes Lord Protector (1653)
Restoration of Charles II (1660)
Bill of Rights passed (1689)

data.title: Order the events leading to the trial and execution of Charles I
items: Second Civil War causes army leaders to distrust Charles I
Pride's Purge removes MPs who oppose the trial (December 1648)
A special High Court of Justice is established (January 1649)
Charles I refuses to recognise the court's authority
Charles I is found guilty
Charles I is executed on 30 January 1649
England becomes a republic called the Commonwealth

data.title: Order the causes that led to the outbreak of the English Civil War in 1642
items: James I claims divine right and clashes with Parliament over money
Charles I collects Ship Money without Parliament's consent
Laud's religious reforms anger Puritans in England and Scotland
Scottish rebellion forces Charles to recall Parliament (1640)
Parliament challenges royal power and passes limiting laws
Charles I attempts to arrest five MPs (January 1642)
Both sides begin preparing for armed conflict
Civil War breaks out at Nottingham (August 1642)
